abstract: The stroma is a heterogenous framework that plays a critical role to mechanically and biologically support contiguous parenchymal elements in any organ. Studies on kidney development have historically focused largely on the epithelial and vascular tissue elements. Recent progress demonstrating stromal cell heterogeneity provided a basis to further investigate stromal functions at the crossroads of mechanical and chemical signaling in genetic mutants with stromal cell deficiency of Integrin-Linked Kinase, a Focal Adhesion (FA) adaptor, and a key regulator of the embryonic kidney. Our data demonstrate disruptions in stromal tissue integrity downstream of Ilk deletion, starting with loss of fibronectin and cellularity and stromal tissue tears, and eventually developing into fluid-filled tissue spaces with stromal cell death. We identified extracellular matrix (ECM) and FA programs as transcriptional and non-transcriptional targets of Ilk deletion and demonstrated that renal stroma normally gains these programs during development, which, when blocked by Ilk deficiency, leads to phenotypes that resemble a developmental arrest. Our data also identify E15.5-E16.5 as a critical developmental window for establishment of these programs.
